title: The Stories That Raised Us
summary: Sometimes you hear yourself speak and realise somebody is still alive in the way you move through the world. Not every inheritance came as a speech. Some came as stories, habits, prayers, jokes, and the ordinary way somebody kept showing up.
excerpt: Sometimes you hear yourself speak and realise somebody is still alive in the way you move through the world. Not every inheritance came as a speech. Some came as stories, habits, prayers, jokes, and the ordinary way somebody kept showing up.
paragraphs: Sometimes you hear yourself say something and realise it did not start with you. It comes out while you are packing lunch, greeting a visitor, calming a child, or trying to make sense of a hard day. A phrase. A warning. A way of laughing at trouble. Suddenly somebody else's voice is alive in yours again.

That is how a lot of us were raised. Not only by rules written down clearly, but by repeated stories, habits, tones, prayers, and ordinary examples that settled into us before we had language for what they were doing. The way tea was offered. The way elders were greeted. The way a person could make very little food stretch and still insist everybody had eaten.

Some inheritances arrive as big memories. A father telling the same story about his first job until the point lodged in you. A mother praying in the next room when money was tight. A grandmother recalling the year things almost fell apart, but somehow the family held. An older sibling teaching you when to keep quiet and when not to let yourself be pushed around.

Other inheritances are easier to miss because they feel so ordinary. The neighbour who knew who had arrived home late. The aunt who made space at her table without making it feel like charity. The teacher who noticed the child who had learnt to disappear. The friend's parent who spoke to you as though your future was already worth taking seriously. Those things do not always look life-changing while they are happening. Years later, you realise they helped teach you what care feels like.

Not everybody was raised in a gentle home, and not every story deserves to be carried forward untouched. Some of us were loved well. Some of us were held together by scattered people doing their best. Some of us learnt tenderness in one place and fear in another. Remembering honestly matters. Gratitude does not require pretending every pattern was healthy.

That is part of growing up too. You start recognising what in you feels inherited. The patience you are grateful for. The silence you are trying to unlearn. The hospitality you want to keep. The harshness you do not want to pass on. The strength that carried your people. The weariness that also sat underneath it. Maturity is not only receiving a story. It is deciding what will travel through you and what will stop with you.

I think that is why these old stories matter. They remind us that we did not make ourselves alone. Even the parts of us that feel most natural were often planted by somebody who may never know how far their influence reached. A word they repeated. A sacrifice they made quietly. A steadiness they kept offering when life would have given them an excuse to become hard.

And then there is the other side of it. We are becoming part of somebody else's memory right now. The way we greet people. The way we speak after a frustrating day. The way we apologise. The way we treat workers, children, parents, friends, and strangers in queues. Someone is learning from us without calling it learning yet.

If a face comes to mind while you read this, stay there for a moment. Send the message if you can. Tell the story at the table before it disappears. Write down the saying that still carries your people. Some of what steadies you today was planted long before you knew how to name it. The good stories are still speaking, and they are asking to be carried carefully.
